Inventory notes:
- Demand is variable, typically 3–4 units/day, with spikes to 7–8; recent observations: 3, 7, 3, 4, 8, 0, 4, 4, 3.
- Stockouts are very expensive (about 3 per day plus lost sales), while holding cost is low (about 0.1 per unit) and each order costs 0.5. Favor maintaining safety stock rather than running near zero.
- Lead time appears to be up to 2 days. Include expected demand during the lead time and a buffer of roughly 3–5 units when deciding orders.
- Avoid delaying replenishment when on-hand inventory is below about 7–8 units, especially if arrivals are small or absent.
- Existing pipeline must be included: arrivals can prevent an order, but do not assume they fully cover demand plus safety stock.
- Ordering only 4 units at very low inventory led to stockouts during an 8-unit-demand day; later replenishment and larger orders reduced stockout risk.
- Counts have matched the system; no evidence of shrinkage or adjustment. Receiving temp staffing is a process-risk note, not proof of inventory error.
- Cycle-count scheduling has no immediate inventory implication.

Inventory notes:
- Demand is variable, generally 3–6 units/day, with spikes of 7–8; recent history includes repeated 5–8 unit days and occasional zero.
- Stockouts are extremely costly (about 3 per unit plus lost sales), while holding cost is low (about 0.1/unit) and ordering costs 0.5. Strongly favor surplus and safety stock.
- Lead time is roughly 2 days. Plan for about 8–12 units of demand through the lead-time window plus a 3–5 unit safety buffer; target position is often at least 12–15 units.
- Recent small orders (3–6 units) failed to recover inventory: stock remained at zero and stockouts persisted across Days 12–20, despite scheduled arrivals. Do not use small “top-up” orders when inventory is depleted.
- When on-hand is below 7–8 units, replenish immediately and aggressively. At zero on hand, order enough to rebuild safety stock, not merely cover the next day.
- Include pipeline arrivals in calculations, but treat them as insufficient/uncertain until they actually arrive. Do not let nominal arrivals justify delaying an order when stock is low.
- Recent average demand is around 4–5/day, with frequent high-demand days; use the upper end of the range for planning.
- Counts have matched the system; no evidence of shrinkage or adjustment. Temporary receiving staff, racking changes, and pickup timing are process-risk notes only, not proof of inventory error.
- Cycle-count scheduling has no immediate inventory implication.

Inventory notes:

- Stockouts are very costly (~3/unit plus lost sales); holding cost is low (~0.1/unit) and ordering cost is 0.5. Favor adequate surplus and safety stock.
- Lead time is about 2 days. Target roughly 12–15 units of inventory position, with additional buffer when recent demand is elevated. At least 15–20 units may be appropriate after depletion or a demand spike.
- Small top-up orders during depletion caused prolonged stockouts (Days 12–20). At zero on hand, order aggressively enough to rebuild safety stock, not merely cover the next day. Day 24’s order of 20, followed by 15-unit orders, successfully restored availability.
- Replenish promptly below about 7–8 units, but include confirmed pipeline arrivals. Days 25–27 show that no new order was needed with 6–20 on hand plus 15–20 arriving; avoid unnecessary orders when the position is adequately protected.
- Treat scheduled arrivals as likely but not fully available until received; do not delay an urgent order solely because nominal arrivals exist when on-hand is critically low.
- After recovery, taper orders rather than continuing emergency quantities: 15 on hand with no pipeline supported a 5-unit order; 9 on hand with 5 arriving supported an 8-unit order.
- Counts have matched the system; no evidence of shrinkage or adjustment. Receiving staff, racking changes, pickup timing, and certification events are process-risk notes only.
- Cycle-count scheduling has no immediate inventory implication.

Inventory notes:
- Demand is variable: baseline roughly 5–6/day, with frequent 7–10 and occasional 14–15 spikes; zero remains possible. Use recent demand and trend, but do not overreact to isolated spikes.
- Stockouts are very costly (~3/unit plus lost sales), while holding (~0.1/unit) and ordering (~0.5/order) are low. Maintain safety stock, but account for all confirmed pipeline.
- Lead time is about 2 days. Evaluate inventory position as on-hand plus scheduled arrivals minus expected demand through lead time. A practical protected position is roughly 12–15 units, increasing after sustained high demand.
- When on-hand is zero or critically low, order enough to rebuild safety stock, even with nominal arrivals. Day 33 still incurred a stockout despite ordering 15; avoid relying on pipeline when immediate supply is inadequate.
- Replenish promptly below about 7–8 units only when the protected inventory position is insufficient. Recent experience shows no order was needed with 9 on hand plus 10 arriving, or 11 on hand plus 6 arriving.
- Avoid unnecessary orders when on-hand and pipeline together provide several days of coverage. Orders on Day 36 (10 units with 21 on hand) and Day 38 (6 with 9 on hand plus 10 arriving) added holding cost without preventing stockouts.
- After recovery, taper orders. Do not continue emergency-sized orders once on-hand and arrivals restore coverage.
- Scheduled arrivals are likely but not available until received; place an urgent order if current stock cannot cover near-term demand.
- Counts have matched the system; no evidence of shrinkage or adjustment. Racking rotation, pickup timing, certification, and cycle counts are process-risk notes only and have not shown inventory impact.

Inventory notes:
- Demand is variable, with baseline roughly 5–6/day, frequent 7–10, and occasional 14–15 spikes; zero is possible. Recent demand has run high (often 8–15), so temporarily raise the forecast/safety stock rather than relying on the long-run baseline.
- Stockouts are very costly (~3/unit plus lost sales), while holding (~0.1/unit) and ordering (~0.5/order) are low. Favor ample safety stock and rebuild decisively after a stockout.

When current stock cannot cover near-term demand, order enough for immediate protection and recovery; do not assume scheduled arrivals prevent today’s stockout.

- Replenish below roughly 7–8 units only after checking near-term demand and confirmed arrivals. Low stock plus pipeline can still be inadequate if today’s demand exceeds on-hand.
- Avoid unnecessary orders when on-hand and arrivals provide several days of coverage; taper after recovery. Holding cost is preferable to repeated stockouts, but do not stack emergency orders once coverage is restored.
- Carrier pickup timing may affect availability; treat arrivals as unavailable until received. Racking rotation, receiving staffing, and cycle counts remain process-risk notes only; no evidence yet of shrinkage or count errors.

Inventory notes:
- Demand is variable: typical 5–10/day, frequent 11–16 spikes, and occasional zero/1. Recent demand remains elevated (14-day average roughly 8–9/day), so use a temporarily higher forecast and safety stock.
- Stockouts are very costly (~3/unit plus lost sales); holding (~0.1/unit) and ordering (~0.5/order) are cheap. Protect against stockouts, but taper decisively once recovery creates several days of coverage.
- Lead time is about 2 days. Evaluate inventory position as on-hand plus confirmed arrivals minus expected demand through lead time, while distinguishing immediately usable stock from pipeline. Treat arrivals as unavailable until received.
- Pipeline is not sufficient when on-hand cannot cover today/next day. Day 55 had only 1 on hand with an arrival of 18 on the following day and still incurred a major stockout; order for the immediate gap and recovery, not merely the pipeline shortfall.
- With zero or near-zero stock, order promptly for roughly the next two days’ demand plus safety stock—often 15–25 units in the current high-demand regime. Avoid tiny follow-up orders that leave no usable stock while waiting.
- Replenish below roughly 7–8 units after checking near-term demand and arrival timing. A recent sale of 16 showed that even 8 on hand can be inadequate; order more aggressively when the latest demand is a spike.
- Once on-hand reaches roughly 25–30+ with no imminent demand risk, stop ordering and let stock deplete. Days 57–60 show that excess inventory creates material holding cost without benefit.
- Receiving temps, carrier timing, racking rotation, and cycle counts are process-risk notes only; counts have matched the system and there is no evidence of shrinkage or count errors.

Inventory notes:
- Demand is variable: typically 5–10/day, with frequent 11–16 spikes and occasional 0–1. The recent 14-day average is about 8/day; use roughly 8–10/day as the baseline, with temporary safety stock for spikes.
- Stockouts are very costly (~$3/unit plus lost sales), but recent decisions produced no stockouts and several holding-cost penalties. Avoid ordering merely to build a large buffer: holding is ~$0.10/unit and each order costs ~$0.50.
- Lead time is about 2 days. Track inventory position as on-hand plus confirmed arrivals minus expected demand through lead time, but treat arrivals as unavailable until received. Pipeline can adequately cover demand when on-hand is moderate; it is not a substitute for immediate stock in a near-zero position.
- With zero/near-zero on-hand and no prompt arrival, order promptly for roughly two days’ demand plus safety stock (often 15–25 units in a high-demand regime). Do not use tiny gap orders that leave no usable stock.
- Replenish cautiously below about 7–8 units, considering arrivals and recent demand. A recent spike justifies more, but 10–12 on hand plus arrivals often needs no order.
- When on-hand is around 17–25 and arrivals are due within two days, usually wait, even after a one-day spike; recent orders at these levels (including 15–18-unit orders) mainly increased holding cost.
- Let inventory deplete rather than maintaining 25–30+ units. Days 68–70 show that ordering while 17–21 on hand and 15–36 incoming created avoidable holding cost.
- Receiving, carrier, racking, temp, and cycle-count notes are process risks only. Counts have matched the system; no evidence of shrinkage or count errors.
